newsitem.title: USA: Cohen confirmed, says U.S. to quit Bosnia in 18 months.
newsitem.headline: Cohen confirmed, says U.S. to quit Bosnia in 18 months.

text.p: William Cohen, a former senator from Maine who served 24 years in Congress, was unanimously confirmed by the Senate on Wednesday as secretary of defence, the first Republican to join President Bill Clinton's Cabinet.

Cohen told the Senate Armed Services Committee at his confirmation hearing that the United States intended to have its troops out of Bosnia in 18 months, even if the Europeans decide to keep their peacekeepers there longer.
He also said he intended to give a new focus to U.S. security relations in Asia because of what he said was a shift there of the world economy's centre of gravity.

The 56-year-old veteran of Congress, who will succeed William Perry as Pentagon chief, is a published poet and spy novelist. He retired from the Senate this month after a career spent largely on defence and intelligence issues.

Considered a moderate in a Republican Party increasingly dominated by conservatives, he was vice chairman of the Senate Intelligence Committee from 1987 to 1991 and of the joint congressional committee that investigated the Iran-Contra affair involving President Ronald Reagan's administration.

At his hearing on Wednesday, Cohen said a U.S. agreement to keep peacekeeping troops in Bosnia another 18 months was a deadline carrying a strong signal to European allies: "We are not going to be there (after 18 months). This is going to end at this point."
He said his first trip as secretary of defence will be to Europe to deliver his message to European allies firsthand.
"This is the kind of issue that can go on too long," Cohen testified. "It (Bosnia) was principally a European problem to be solved ... it is time for them to assume responsibility."

The United States has 8,500 troops in a second round of a NATO-led peacekeeping mission in Bosnia, a commitment scheduled to end in 18 months. Many Republicans sharply criticised Clinton's decision to return U.S. troops to Bosnia after his original commitment to do so for just one year.

Cohen said the United States will examine its troop commitment in Bosnia every six months and he expected the U.S. contribution to come down significantly within a year and "that we would be out at the end of that 18 months."

But outgoing Defence Secretary Perry, who is leaving after three years on the job, was much more careful about any future U.S. commitment in Bosnia in an interview with Reuters shortly after Cohen was confirmed.

"That's going to be an issue for the President and the secretary to debate at that time. I wouldn't want to try to forecast what the judgment would be a year and a-half from now," added Perry, who assured Congress before the first deployment in late 1985 that the Bosnia mission would last only a year.
Cohen, meanwhile, stressed that the Asia-Pacific region was an important one.

"I intend to give new focus to our security relations in the Asia-Pacific region. As the centre of gravity of the world economy has shifted to the Pacific, our increasing economic integration with Asia's dynamic economies has created enormous opportunities for American businesses and workers," he said.
"Beyond the near-term threat from North Korea, our interests are potentially jeopardised by the danger of instability and rivalry among major region powers," he said.

The United States must keep and expand its security engagement in Asia while continuing policies in Europe, Russia, East Asia and Southwest Asia that are "critical to protecting and promoting America's interests in the new century," he said.
The United States is worried about continued friction between India and Pakistan and is seeking to forge closer ties with China despite differences over human rights and trade.
